dse-p4-pp-2015-1-1-selfies.source_note: Past-paper practice based on the verified 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.1 task. context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.1:
context.title: Four Ways to Improve a Selfie
body: A school photography club is comparing four tools for taking selfies. A small wireless shutter lets users place a phone at a distance and take a picture without touching it. A camera app offers a timer and simple editing features. A lightweight selfie stick can include more people or more of the background in a photograph.

The fourth option is a smartphone designed for self-portraits. Its rotating camera makes unusual angles easier, while a beauty setting changes skin tone and face shape. The products range from a low-cost app to an expensive phone, so price, portability and picture quality do not point to the same choice.

Club members must recommend only two items for students. They should consider why young people enjoy selfies, whether editing encourages creativity or unrealistic images, and whether a gadget will still be useful after the novelty disappears. A strong recommendation should identify the intended users and explain why each chosen tool offers good value.

part_a.instruction: As members of your school's Photography Club, give a talk about selfies and recommend two pieces of equipment for taking better selfies. Discuss the following points.

discussion_points.text: Why selfies seem to be so popular among young people
The advantages and disadvantages of the gadgets advertised
Which two you would recommend
Anything else you think is important

Do you post selfies on social media sites?
Do you prefer to take a selfie or ask a friend to take a photo of you?
Do you have a favourite photo of yourself?
Do you prefer to take a selfie of yourself or with other people?
Why do you think some people like selfies?
Why do you think selfies are more popular among younger people than older people?
Do you think the selfie is a form of creative expression or self-love?

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.2:
context.title: A School Memory Box for the Moon
body: A private space project plans to bury a digital archive beneath the surface of the moon. Part of the archive will record major events from human history, while another part will contain memory boxes made by families, schools and community groups. Each box may hold photographs, recordings, short videos, poems or personal messages.

Your school has been offered one box. Some students want it to celebrate the school anniversary, using old class photos, songs and interviews with former teachers. Others prefer a theme about student life today, including lunchtime conversations, club activities and hopes for the future. Storage space is limited, so not every suggestion can be accepted.

The Student Union also wants the project to involve more than a small committee. Possible ideas include an online vote, a memory-collection week and recording booths at school. The final selection should represent different ages and experiences, protect personal privacy and remain understandable to someone who discovers it many years from now.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.3:
context.title: Sport, Learning and Olympic Values
body: The Youth Olympic Games brings together athletes aged fifteen to eighteen, but competition is only one part of the event. Its wider aim is to promote respect, excellence and friendship. At one recent Games, young athletes met experienced champions, explored career planning and joined interactive sessions about fair play, first aid and global issues.

A school Sports Society wants to adapt these ideas for local students. A conversation with athletes could make sports careers feel real, while a time-management workshop might help students balance training and study. An international exhibition could reach a larger audience, although it would require more research, displays and volunteers.

The society must decide which activities suit secondary students and how people outside the school can take part. It could invite community coaches, organise mixed-age teams or connect activities with a charity. Whatever it chooses, the programme should welcome beginners, value sportsmanship as much as winning, and give participants a meaningful role rather than making them passive spectators.

Why do some athletes only care about winning?
Which is more important: winning the game or sportsmanship?
Do you agree that athletes should be role models for teenagers?
Do you think it is a good idea to pursue a career in sports in Hong Kong?
Why is it important to promote sports culture in Hong Kong?

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.1:
context.title: Repairing Toys and Preserving Memories
body: A family-run workshop has repaired dolls, teddy bears and wheeled toys for several generations. Its craftspeople treat each object differently because materials, age and damage vary. Many customers are adults who want to restore a childhood toy, pass it to a younger relative or preserve a reminder of someone important.

The business also sells replacement clothing, accessories and collectible dolls. Repairs can be slow and expensive because experienced workers must clean fragile materials, recreate missing parts and explain what can safely be restored. However, customers may value the emotional history of an object more than the price of buying a new toy.

Business Studies students are considering whether a similar service could succeed in Hong Kong. They need to identify likely customers, suitable prices and ways to build trust. Social-media before-and-after videos, partnerships with toy shops and repair workshops for families could attract attention, but rent, specialist training and a limited market may make the idea risky.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.2:
context.title: Four Practical Electives
body: A secondary school is considering four new electives for senior students. Firefighting would teach safety, teamwork and emergency procedures through demanding practical activities. Media Technology and Film Production would cover planning, filming, interviewing and editing. Both courses could build confidence, although they require specialist equipment and trained instructors.

Fisheries and Wildlife Management would introduce local species, habitats and conservation, with learning outside the classroom. Business Law would explore contracts, consumer rights, employment and the legal responsibilities of individuals and companies. These subjects may connect school learning with future careers, but not every student will find the same course useful or attractive.

Only one course can begin next year. The Student Union must compare educational value, popularity, safety, cost and timetable pressure. It should also consider whether students without previous experience can participate fairly. A trial lesson or interest survey may provide evidence, but the final recommendation should explain how the course benefits students beyond simply being new or entertaining.

context.title: Training for a Future Mission to Mars
body: Alyssa Carson became interested in Mars while still a child and began attending science and space camps. She studies several languages, follows a demanding school programme and takes part in training designed to build fitness, teamwork and problem-solving skills. Her long-term ambition is to join a crewed mission to Mars.

Supporters say her determination can show students that a distant goal becomes more realistic when it is divided into small steps. Space travel also involves isolation, risk and many years of specialised preparation.

The Astronomy Club would like to invite Alyssa to school. Members must explain why her experience is relevant, choose topics for her talk and plan activities that involve the audience. A question-and-answer session, a mission-planning challenge or a small science exhibition could work, provided the visit discusses setbacks and uncertainty as honestly as ambition and success.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 3.1:
context.title: Should Students Bring Their Own Devices?
body: A school is considering allowing students to bring smartphones, tablets or notebook computers into selected lessons. Teachers who volunteer would test the policy first, before the school decides whether to expand it. Supporters believe students could research information quickly, create multimedia work and use accessibility tools suited to their needs.

The policy also raises practical problems. Not every family can afford the same device or data plan, and students may become distracted by messages, games or social media. Teachers would need clear rules for appropriate use, secure charging and online safety. Printed materials should remain available when technology fails or is unsuitable.

Before making a recommendation, students should identify the subjects in which a personal device adds genuine learning value. They should also propose ways to lend equipment, protect privacy and respond to misuse without disrupting the whole class. The aim is not to replace teachers or books, but to decide when technology makes learning more effective and inclusive.

context.title: Five Careers with Different Strengths
body: A careers survey highlights five occupations with different skill demands: software developer, market researcher, physiotherapist, interpreter and nutritionist. Some rely heavily on technology or data, while others require close communication with clients. All involve solving problems, continuing to learn and explaining specialised knowledge in a clear way.

Students may be attracted by salary, job opportunities or the chance to help people. However, a popular career can still involve long training, irregular hours or intense competition. A university degree is essential for some roles but not the only route into every industry. Personal interest matters, yet it must be considered alongside ability and working conditions.

The Careers Committee wants its workshop to move beyond job titles. It could include short role-play tasks, a skills-matching quiz and conversations with people working in different sectors. The group should decide which skills to feature, predict which jobs students will find attractive and ensure the workshop helps participants question assumptions instead of simply following a ranking.

context.title: A Vertical City in One Building
body: Architects have proposed an 'Endless City': a three-hundred-metre building containing homes, offices, shops, parks and entertainment areas. Ramps, bridges and public spaces would connect its levels, allowing residents to move between daily activities without travelling across the city. Supporters argue that vertical development could use scarce urban land more efficiently.

Living in one giant structure might reduce commuting and make services convenient. Shared gardens and gathering areas could also encourage contact between residents. On the other hand, the project may feel crowded or artificial, and people could become dependent on a complex building for transport, safety, energy and essential services.

The proposal is being considered as an idea for Hong Kong. The discussion should identify missing facilities, compare the benefits and drawbacks of daily life inside the building and judge whether residents would accept it. Cost, emergency planning, access to sunlight and the need for open public space are as important as its dramatic appearance.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 8.1:
context.title: Does Fame Affect Justice?
body: News reports often give great attention to celebrities who break the law. Some receive fines, treatment programmes or community service and later rebuild their careers. Supporters of rehabilitation argue that famous people deserve the same chance to change as anyone else. Their cases may also draw public attention to the consequences of illegal behaviour.

Others believe fame creates unfair advantages. Expensive legal support, loyal fans and public sympathy may influence how a case is discussed, even when courts apply the same rules. At the same time, demanding a harsher sentence simply because someone is well known would also conflict with equal treatment under the law.

The Liberal Studies Society is considering punishment, public reaction and continued fan support. The group should separate legal penalties from moral expectations and avoid assuming that every case is alike. It should discuss whether celebrities have extra responsibility as role models, while recognising that admiration for a person’s work does not excuse harmful conduct.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2015 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 8.2:
context.title: When Should Formal Schooling Begin?
body: Some education researchers argue that children under six need more time for play, movement and social development before beginning full classroom instruction. They warn that pressure to read, write and complete formal tasks too early may create anxiety and leave less time for curiosity, independence and learning through experience.

Other specialists point out that a well-designed early programme can provide language support, regular routines and access to trained adults. Children from families with fewer resources may particularly benefit. The important distinction may be between developmentally appropriate early education and a narrow programme dominated by worksheets, testing and long periods of sitting.

A debate on school starting age should therefore examine both timing and the kind of education offered. The group must present arguments for and against the motion, decide which side to support and respond to differences between children. Parental choice, government standards, equality of access and the meaning of “formal schooling” should all be clarified.

context.title: Sit Less, Move More?
body: Many students and office workers spend most of the day sitting. Standing desks allow users to raise the work surface and change position without leaving a task. Supporters say alternating between sitting and standing can reduce stiffness, encourage movement and make people more aware of long periods of inactivity.

A standing desk is not a complete health solution. Standing for too long can cause discomfort, and desks may be expensive or difficult to fit into crowded rooms. Height must be adjusted correctly, while students with particular health needs may require other arrangements. Evidence about concentration and long-term benefits should not be exaggerated.

A class presentation should explain both advantages and disadvantages and show how the desks might be used safely. A short demonstration, posture comparison or audience poll could make the topic engaging. The key message should be flexible movement rather than replacing all sitting with standing, and any school trial should gather feedback from different users.

context.title: Building Connections Across Generations
body: An Adopt-A-Grandparent programme connects students with older volunteers from their families or the local community. Participants might read together, share traditional skills, record neighbourhood memories or work on school projects. Regular contact can reduce loneliness and help students understand experiences very different from their own.

The relationship should not present older people only as people who need help. Many have professional knowledge, practical skills and time to contribute. Students can offer companionship and digital support, while grandparents can provide guidance and stories. Careful matching is needed because interests, mobility, language and availability will vary.

A school considering the programme must decide what volunteers will do, how students and the school will benefit and how meetings will be organised. Consent, safeguarding, transport and staff supervision are essential. The programme should begin with clear expectations and a trial period, then use feedback from both generations to improve activities and avoid one-sided or uncomfortable relationships.
